title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to test whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. Execution used declared model gpt-5-mini and a deterministic network validator under shared_initial_candidate semantics (exactly one initial LLM generation per task, reused across arms); guarded episodes could request up to one validator‑triggered repair. We ran N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial). All tasks were scored safe under both arms (baseline safe = 240/240; guarded safe = 240/240). The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Notably, under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the paired contrast could only differ if the shared initial candidate failed validation or a validator‑triggered repair was applied; because every shared candidate passed validation and no repairs were invoked, the paired contrast is degenerate and uninformative about downstream repair efficacy in this run. We report the preregistered design, numeric execution accounting, artifact‑grounded analysis, an evidence‑based explanation for the null paired outcome, and concrete recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction:
Translating high‑level operator intent into concrete device configurations with minimal human intervention is a core NetOps objective. Large language models (LLMs) offer flexible intent‑to‑configuration translation, but textual fidelity metrics do not capture ordering, dependency, or invariant violations that can make a set of commands unsafe when applied to running network elements. Emulation‑grounded, closed‑loop evaluation—where generated configurations are applied to device images or simulators and scored by deterministic checks—exposes semantic failure modes (incorrect sequencing, transient violations, unauthorized resource touches) that text‑only tests miss.

A recurring architectural pattern to reduce such semantic failures is generate–validate–repair (GVR): an LLM proposes a candidate configuration, a deterministic verifier checks semantic constraints, and an automated repair routine rewrites the candidate when violations are detected. Prior work documents GVR‑style designs and prototype benefits on benchmarked faults, but open empirical questions remain about whether and when deterministic verifiers measurably reduce unsafe applications under distribution shift and adversarial prompts, and how evaluation semantics (e.g., whether paired arms share the same initial LLM sample) affect inferential value. We preregistered and executed a paired experiment to measure the absolute paired difference in unsafe‑apply rate (guarded minus baseline) under a shared_initial_candidate execution contract. Our contributions are: (1) an artifact‑grounded report of a preregistered paired GVR experiment with full numeric accounting; (2) explicit mapping from the preregistered estimand to archived analysis outputs and exact numeric results; and (3) an artifact‑grounded failure analysis explaining the observed null paired contrast and recommendations for experiments that can produce informative paired differences.
sections.related_work: Executable NetOps benchmarks and emulation frameworks have recently been proposed to examine end‑to‑end agentic behavior rather than only textual outputs; NetConfArena is a representative executable, closed‑loop benchmark that motivates emulation‑grounded evaluation. Research on automated configuration repair and program repair documents generate–validate patterns and shows that validators can enable high repair coverage for many syntactic and some semantic faults, while emphasizing that verifier semantic coverage is a key limiter. Surveys and position papers synthesize agentic architectures, tool augmentation, verifier integration, and uncertainty calibration as promising patterns for operational NetOps automation and safety. Work on configuration analysis tools (e.g., Batfish evolution) provides engineering precedent for verifier design and incremental verification. Our study differs by combining a preregistered paired estimand, shared_initial_candidate semantics, emulation‑grounded deterministic scoring, and archival of per‑call and validator traces so that every principal numeric claim can be reconciled to archived artifacts.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01). The primary estimand is paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, defined as the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline) where unsafe_apply = 1 denotes a final configuration that would cause a semantic safety violation when applied. The analysis used a paired binary executor with bootstrap percentile CIs (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) and an exact two‑sided McNemar test for discordant pairs.

Design and sampling: The design is paired with shared_initial_candidate generation semantics: the adapter produced exactly one initial LLM generation per task and both arms observed that same generation; the guarded arm could request up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. We executed N = 240 distinct intent→configuration tasks blocked into topology/vendor clusters: in‑distribution = 144, distribution‑shift = 48, adversarial‑prompt = 48. Tasks were generated deterministically by a registered task generator and include explicit initial states, required command sequences, and constraints to make semantic correctness checkable in the emulator.

Models, verifier, and adapter contract: Execution used the declared model gpt-5-mini. The deterministic verifier implements a finite set of semantic checks for sequencing, protected interfaces, minimal availability constraints, and field‑change preconditions; the guarded pipeline was permitted up to one deterministic repair invocation per task. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics, paired differences can only arise if the single shared initial candidate fails deterministic validation or the guarded arm successfully applies a repair that changes the final configuration compared to baseline.

Scoring, exclusions, and missingness: Final outcomes are binary (safe vs unsafe) determined by deterministic emulation and invariant checks. Preregistered exclusions included items flagged as possible false‑safe (validator PASS but emulator reports unsafe) and infra failures after allowed retries; in such cases sensitivity analyses were declared. The retry policy permitted up to two automatic infra retries per task. All counting and missingness rules were applied per the preregistration and archived.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: The run completed according to the preregistered plan. Planned episode count = 480; completed episode count = 480; complete pairs = 240. Exactly one shared initial generation was produced per task (model calls used = 240 under the shared‑candidate contract). No infra failures, no unscorable episodes, and no preregistered exclusions occurred.

Primary outcomes and contingency: Every paired episode was scored safe in both arms. Baseline successes = 240 of 240 (baseline unsafe_apply = 0); guarded successes = 240 of 240 (guarded unsafe_apply = 0). The paired contingency is n11 = 240 (both safe), n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The paired estimator (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0.

Validator activity and repair utilization: Across the experiment no validator‑triggered repairs were applied (repair attempts = 0). Representative archived validator traces record validation‑before and validation‑after snapshots, required command counts, and difficulty labels; these traces confirm that the shared initial candidates satisfied the deterministic checks in every task. Consequently, the guarded pipeline did not exercise the repair path and could not produce discordant paired outcomes.

Planned sensitivity channels: The preregistration included sensitivity analyses for possible false‑safe flags and infra failures, and subgroup contrasts by task condition (in‑distribution, shift, adversarial). Because no flags or infra failures occurred and all paired outcomes are identical, subgroup contrasts are degenerate; archived subgroup summaries reflect zero unsafe applies in every subgroup.
sections.discussion:
Mechanistic explanation of the null paired contrast: By design, shared_initial_candidate semantics produce exactly one LLM sample per task reused by both arms; under that contract the guarded arm only differs from baseline if the shared candidate fails deterministic validation or if a validator‑triggered repair is applied and changes the final configuration. In this execution every shared candidate passed the deterministic checks and no repairs were invoked, so the guarded arm could not change any paired outcome. This mechanistic account is supported by the numeric execution accounting and archived validator traces and explains the degenerate contingency table.

Design tradeoffs and implications for inference: Shared_initial_candidate semantics reduce model‑call budget and ensure direct sample pairing, but they also constrain the experiment's ability to detect verifier benefit because generator variability between arms is eliminated. To obtain informative paired contrasts for verifier efficacy, future experiments should consider one or more of: (A) allowing independent initial generations per arm (so the verifier can veto harmful LLM outputs that would otherwise have been accepted in baseline), (B) increasing adversary strength or introducing controlled generator perturbations to create more validation failures, or (C) expanding repair budgets (allow multiple repair iterations) and instrumenting repair traces to study repair search behavior. Each option trades compute and experimental complexity against power to observe discordant pairs.

Threats to validity (artifact‑grounded): Internal validity: the shared_initial_candidate contract is an explicit design choice that restricts causal contrast interpretation; its runtime adherence is reflected in the execution accounting. Construct validity: the deterministic verifier encodes a finite check set and may not cover all semantic fault classes; verifier PASS vs real‑world effect mismatches remain possible in broader deployments. External validity: tasks were drawn from a synthetic emulation corpus and a deterministic task generator; extrapolation to production, heterogeneous vendor ecosystems, operator processes, and adaptive adversaries requires caution. Conclusion validity: the observed baseline unsafe rate = 0 prevents detecting verifier benefit under this design; future power analyses should anticipate baseline rates conditional on generation variability and adversary strength.

Recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations: avoid shared_initial_candidate when the primary goal is to estimate verifier causal effect; increase repair iteration budgets and record repair edits; strengthen or diversify adversary generation protocols; and expand verifier semantic coverage and cross‑checks between verifier PASS and emulator outcomes to detect potential false‑safe cases.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a GVR pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration. Numeric outcome: every paired episode was safe under both arms, yielding a paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). Crucially, under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the paired contrast could only differ if the single shared initial candidate failed deterministic validation or if a validator‑triggered repair was applied; in this run the shared initial candidates passed validation and no repairs were invoked, producing the degenerate paired outcome. We present the preregistered design, exact numeric accounting, and an artifact‑grounded failure analysis that identifies how future experiments can be configured to produce informative paired contrasts for verifier efficacy.

The study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01; preregistration SHA‑256: 3e73ca0dc935a8754bf2dfbe6869ff989c47f1db0d93e2ca34809be8ebf95e26). The initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Human role and autonomy boundary: prior to the autonomy lock the human Research Director selected the topic family and constrained the initial master prompt; all literature search, experiment design, preregistration, execution, analysis, and manuscript drafting were performed autonomously after the lock. The registered execution semantics used shared_initial_candidate (one shared initial generation per task reused across both arms); under that contract paired divergences require validator failure of the shared candidate or a validator‑triggered repair. Archived execution and analysis artifacts (execution manifest, per‑call traces, task manifests, validator traces, and analysis CSVs) are preserved in the study archive and provide the provenance for all reported numeric results. No manual human editing of the technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus and deterministic task generator; external validity to production multi‑vendor deployments and operational workflows is limited.
Single model: a single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was used; results do not imply generality across models, prompting strategies, or fine‑tuning.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were produced under a preregistered fixed protocol and do not represent unconstrained or adaptive adversaries.

Verifier coverage: the deterministic verifier encodes a finite check set; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected, and verifier PASS does not guarantee absence of every real‑world failure mode.
